cards.title: Seed the opportunity before assigning the challenge
cards.summary: Show people a concrete need or market gap first so they generate the demand for change themselves instead of receiving a directive.
cards.use_when: Setting strategic direction for a store — entering a new category, repositioning the brand, or launching an offsite planning session.
steps: Before announcing a goal, put the raw material in front of the team: the customer complaint file, the competitor's new listing, the session recordings where shoppers abandon your PDP, the vendor quote that changes unit economics.
Pose hard questions rather than answers: 'Why are we in this category?', 'Do we deserve to be in it?', 'What would it take to beat the leader?'
Expect the questions to stir chaos and tension — the source describes a Korean consumer electronics CEO who never backed down from this discomfort and let the tension force answers out of the team.
Do not supply the answers yourself; the point is to shift the burden of thinking to the group so they own the conclusion.
Seed the opportunity broadly — include executives, family owners, outside advisors — so the eventual plan has more than one sponsor.
caveats: The source's example is a large corporate division; small stores can run the same conversation with 3-5 people.
Seeding without a later deadline and decision rule produces endless discussion.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Ask for a 30 percent answer in two days
cards.summary: Stage high-stakes strategic answers in rough increments — 30% fast, 50% next, 100% over months — to keep momentum while preserving rigor.
cards.use_when: Deciding on a major store change (new category, replatform, new pricing model, new market) where analysis could otherwise stall for weeks.
steps: Frame the levels explicitly: 'I need a 30 percent answer in two days so we can decide whether it's worth finding a 50 percent answer, and if it is, we'll block two months for the 100 percent answer.'
Set a tight, non-negotiable timeline for the rough pass; the source's example was two days.
Treat the rough pass as a decision gate, not a final plan — its job is to reveal whether deeper work is warranted.
Do not wait for full certainty before making the go/no-go call; partial answers that are discussed generate more than polished decks that arrive late.
Apply the same increments to store experiments: rough hypothesis → directional data → full rollout plan.
caveats: The 30/50/100 bands are the source's illustrative heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Skipping the later 100 percent stage leaves you executing on a guess.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Helicopter down: make the stretch target believable
cards.summary: Bring an ambitious goal from 30,000 feet to 1,000 feet with a visible proof point, because a challenge that stays abstract never produces belief.
cards.use_when: Selling the team on a stretch goal — aggressive growth, a new market, a complete site redesign — where you need people to actually commit rather than nod.
steps: State the direction so it is 'improbable but not impossible' — in the source, Bloom Energy's CEO describes a target at half the carbon emissions of traditional generators.
Do not ask the team to pursue something the leadership exposure is only at the 30,000-foot level; the source calls that irresponsible.
Take it down to ground level: show a pathway and show why it can be done — a working prototype, a test page that converts, one supplier who agreed to terms.
The source argues you only need to do this once to create belief, so pick the single most convincing demonstration rather than a long list.
Once belief exists, stop re-selling it; the source says commitment comes from the challenge itself, not from the leader whipping up enthusiasm.
caveats: A proof point must be genuinely representative of the goal, not a stunt separated from the real work.
Belief without a laid-out path reverts to skepticism at the first setback.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Lay out a path instead of issuing an outrageous challenge
cards.summary: Before challenging the team to a seemingly impossible target, analyze historical data to find the repeatable 90 percent that makes it feasible.
cards.use_when: Setting aggressive operational or merchandising targets — seven-day fulfillment, a 24-hour product launch, a much lower return rate.
steps: State the outrageous target first: in the source, SAP's Shai Agassi challenged the team to let a mid-size company install SAP in under seven days when implementations normally take months.
Then analyze historical instances (prior implementations, past launches, existing order data) to find the common structure.
In the source's example, 90 percent of implementations shared the same features and one configuration worked for most mid-size companies — that insight was the path.
Show the team the path you found and let them own execution; the target plus the path becomes repeatable instead of heroic.
Apply this to store operations: before demanding same-day dispatch, identify how many current orders already meet the criteria and what makes those orders different.
caveats: The source's 90 percent figure is from one company's implementation data, not a general benchmark.
A path that only works for a subset of cases should be declared as such.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Co-create the plan to manufacture commitment
cards.summary: People who build the plan believe in its viability far more than people who receive it, which is the real source of collective will to execute.
cards.use_when: Major store initiatives that require cross-functional effort — a replatform, a new pricing architecture, an omnichannel fulfillment change.
steps: Give the group the raw problem and let them construct the strategy rather than handing down a finished plan for feedback.
The source cites Oracle under Ray Lane in 1996, where 250 senior leaders co-created corporate strategy and therefore already understood the necessary actions.
Use the co-created plan to build both understanding and energy: the group leaves knowing what to do and why it is achievable.
Keep the leader's role as convener and final decision-maker, not as the author of every element.
If you cannot co-create the whole plan, co-create the sequencing and trade-offs so people still own the how.
caveats: Co-creation is slow and unsuitable for small tactical decisions.
Co-creation without a clear decision rule (who decides, by when) degrades into an unbounded workshop.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Orchestrate a visible early win en masse
cards.summary: Use a small, visible first success that the whole organization can see together to generate belief for the larger stretch.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a large, risky store initiative such as a new fulfillment model, a loyalty program, or a category expansion.
steps: Resist tackling many problems at once; the source's research found multipliers begin with small early wins and build belief from them.
Do the win en masse and visibly rather than in an isolated pilot that only management notices — the source warns that secluded pilots fail to capture the whole organization.
Concrete examples from the book: hold an open house for a conference-room pilot of new technology, or win back one important customer through a cross-functional team effort.

The source's Green Belt example: Wangari Maathai started with tree planting because it was understandable, doable, inexpensive, and required little technology — and it became the entry point for governance, rights, and resource issues.
For a store: treat one improved product page or one recovered supplier relationship as the entry point, then extend to the harder work.
caveats: The Green Belt's 40 million trees came from decades of community movement — treat that as an illustrative outcome, not a timeline you can copy.
A visible early win that is later abandoned damages belief more than no win at all.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Stop answering, start asking
cards.summary: Shift from answer mode to question mode to draw out what the organization already knows and to transfer ownership of the problem.
cards.use_when: Running meetings on pricing, assortment, merchandising, or site changes where you habitually supply the answer first.
steps: Before each meeting, identify the questions that would surface assumptions and trade-offs, and commit to leading with those.
Lead at least one meeting using only questions; the source describes an extreme version where a friend challenged the author to speak to her children only in questions for an hour or two.

Sequence practical questions: 'What time is it?' → 'What do we do at bedtime?' → 'Who is ready?' — the source's evening example shows each question produces the next action from the people themselves.
Apply the same to a store review: 'What does this data say?' → 'What would have to be true for this to work?' → 'Who is going to do it, and by when?'
Back off after asking; the source says laying down a challenge includes leaving space for people to think through the answers and take ownership.
caveats: The source suggests starting at 100 percent questions to break the habit, then settling into a comfortable level rather than never making statements.
Rhetorical 'gotcha' questions that test people's knowledge are the Diminisher pattern and destroy safety.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Take a bus trip to make the need visible
cards.summary: Move the team physically to where the customer or market problem is visible, and let the group generate the new ideas themselves.
cards.use_when: Product selection and merchandising planning, when the team is optimizing existing listings and missing a market shift.
steps: Load the whole relevant team — in the source, GE's Tom Tiller took forty managers on a rented bus to the Atlanta Kitchen and Bath Show to find trends and needs.
Give the group a clear brief: identify trends and needs, then generate new product ideas.
In the source, the group developed a new line of products and turned the failing appliance division from a large loss to a $10 million profit.
Adapt for ecommerce: physically visit a customer's warehouse to watch them use the product, or go together to a mall or market to watch people shop.
The key instruction is to go together — the shared learning experience reveals the need, creates energy, and ignites the organization rather than one person returning with findings.
caveats: The GE turnaround result is a case example, not a guaranteed outcome.
A bus trip without a clear question produces tourism, not insight.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Know-It-All direction creates idle cycles
cards.summary: When leadership hands down directives that showcase their own knowledge, people stop thinking, wait for decisions, and the organization slows to the speed of one person.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow store decision cycles — price changes, listing approvals, promotional calendars that stall waiting on the owner.
steps: Watch for the three Diminisher behaviors: telling what they know without inviting contribution, testing what others know via gotcha questions, and telling people exactly how to do their jobs.
Recognize the symptom in people: the source quotes a VP who spent most of his time waiting for his boss's decisions, effectively working part time, bored, and taking sailing lessons.
Recognize the deeper cost: the organization burns energy deducing what the boss thinks instead of advancing the work.
Change the behavior by defining opportunities that challenge people to go beyond what they know how to do, rather than instructions.
Watch for the case where expertise is bypassed: in the source's film example, the director of photography resigned mid-shoot because the executive producer kept telling staff how to light shots.
caveats: Raw expertise is still relevant; the source's claim is that leaders who only direct from their own knowledge cap the organization at what they personally know.
Some decisions legitimately need top-down direction and should not be opened to debate.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Challengers get faster cycles than directive bosses
cards.summary: Teams that understand the challenge can act without waiting for the leader, producing accelerated problem-solving and discretionary effort.
cards.use_when: Setting up store operations, marketing calendars, or product-launch cadence so day-to-day decisions don't bottleneck on the owner.
steps: Define the overarching opportunity clearly and repeatedly so people understand the context well enough to act on their own.
Expect the payoff the source describes: rapid cycles and accelerated problem solving without the formal leader initiating each step.

Contrast the two patterns from the book: Know-It-Alls get distracted efforts as people vie for the boss's attention, idle cycles, and an organization that doesn't want to get ahead of the boss; Challengers get collective intent, rapid cycles, and discretionary effort on the toughest challenges.

Create room for fast work by not punishing mistakes: the source quotes a CTO at Better Place who said he did more in one year there than in twenty years previously because he wasn't punished for mistakes.
Track whether your team is waiting on you; waiting time is the measurable symptom of the directive pattern.
caveats: The Better Place productivity comparison is one person's testimony, not a measured study.
Speed without shared context produces uncoordinated activity, not acceleration.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Decide when a decision needs debate and when it doesn't
cards.summary: Multipliers reserve collective debate for decisions of consequence, then run rigorous debate that prosecutes issues with facts and depersonalizes the outcome.
cards.use_when: Choosing which store decisions to make solo (SKU copy edits, daily ad adjustments) and which to open up (pricing model, category entry, fulfillment change).
steps: Apply the source's rule directly: not all decisions need collective input and debate, but decisions of consequence do.
The Microsoft education-business example shows the scale: a decision about redirecting a $300 million business from corporate training to the academic market warranted months of structured debate.

For high-stakes decisions, bring in every relevant insight — the source describes a leader who, after a twelve-hour debate, insisted the team hear one more comment from a junior member, which proved to be the crucial insight.
Depersonalize by attacking the issues, not the people, and keep the discussion fact-based rather than opinion-based.
After the debate, make the decision or explicitly delegate it, then communicate the decision and the rationale.
caveats: Debating everything slows the organization; the source explicitly limits debate to decisions of consequence.
Reserve the right to decide: the exchange of views is not the decision itself.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Frame the issue before the debate
cards.summary: The quality of a debate is determined before it starts: define the question, form the team, assemble the data, and state how the decision will be made.
cards.use_when: Preparing any consequential store decision meeting — pricing change, category expansion, budget cut, vendor switch.
steps: Define the question so it unearths entrenching assumptions, surfaces fundamental tensions and trade-offs, forces people to confront facts, and ensures multiple perspectives.
Form the team from three groups: those with knowledge needed, key stakeholders for the decision, and those responsible for driving the outcome.

Assemble the data in advance and require people to come armed with it; the source describes Tim Cook's team knowing opinions must be informed by fact, not anecdote, with one member bringing a box of backup data.
Frame the decision explicitly: the What (the question), the Why (what in the environment prompts it and the stakes), and the How (timeline, who recommends, who decides).

In the source's Microsoft budget example, Lutz Ziob opened with the tough question — what is the best way to take 20 percent out of the budget — shared openly why HQ requested it, then said each person must explain where the money should come from before he made the final call.
caveats: Framing demands foresight and preparation time; skipping it produces spinning on tangential issues.
Leaving the decision process ambiguous invites people to fill the vacuum with speculation.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Run debate with both safety and rigor
cards.summary: Create the conditions for people's best thinking by removing fear, then demand evidence and challenge assumptions so the debate stays reality-based.
cards.use_when: Facilitating debate on contested store topics — feature additions, discounting policy, ad spend allocation, assortment cuts.
steps: Safety practices: share your view last after hearing others, encourage an opposing stand, invite all points of view, focus on facts, depersonalize issues, and look beyond hierarchy and job titles.

Rigor practices: ask the hard questions, challenge underlying assumptions, demand evidence in the data, attack issues not people, ask 'why' repeatedly to reach root cause, and debate both sides equally.
Switch sides explicitly when discussion settles; the source's Lutz Ziob told two people to swap positions so the issues got pounded from the other vantage point.
Assign functional perspectives: ask someone to debate from marketing instead of technical, or domestic instead of international, to break their usual frame.

The source's online-distribution example: when the team supported adding a store feature on intuition, the CEO demanded sales data, then country-by-country analysis, until the group concluded they lacked enough information and identified what data they needed.
caveats: Opinion-based arguments should not be treated as evidence; Jim Barksdale's line in the source was 'If you don't have any facts, we'll just use my opinion.'
Safety without rigor produces comfortable agreement; rigor without safety produces silence.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Break group agreement by demanding evidence and switching roles
cards.summary: When the team converges too quickly, step back and have someone argue the other side or dig past the summary into segment-level data before deciding.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether to add a site feature, launch a promotion, or change a PDP layout when everyone on the call already agrees.
steps: Notice premature agreement and deliberately interrupt it rather than accepting the consensus.
Ask someone to argue the opposing position or make the argument yourself; the source says multipliers make sure all the rocks are turned over.

Push past summary analysis: in the source's European online distribution example, the CEO insisted the team go country by country through the data to answer whether the feature would actually drive higher sales.
Accept that the honest end of a rigorous debate may be 'we don't have enough information yet' — the source's group landed there and identified the additional data required.
Make the debate educational rather than competitive: the source's criteria say people should leave more focused on what they learned than on who won.
caveats: Role-switching can feel awkward; the source notes the awkwardness passes after a moment or two.
Rigorous debate takes longer and is not warranted for small decisions.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx

cards.title: Reach past hierarchy to include frontline insight in high-stakes decisions
cards.summary: For consequential decisions, gather data and insight from the people closest to the problem rather than only from management, then decide and communicate.
cards.use_when: A recall, a rate-limiting quality problem, a major return-rate spike, or any customer-facing failure that requires a public decision.
steps: Go directly to the people who understand the issue and tell them you need their input, rather than relying solely on your own read of the situation.
The Affymetrix example: president Sue Siegel learned from customers that GeneChip microarrays could produce inaccurate results for a minor portion of applications and had to decide on a recall.

Convene a forum across several layers of management, frame the magnitude of the issue and its potential impact, lay out a couple of scenarios, and then ask questions across angles: impact on customers, legal obligation, financial impact.
Ask for data and recommendations, then hold the debate — in the source, two arduous days — before asking the management team to weigh in and making the decision.
Communicate the decision and rationale openly: Siegel personally presented the mistake and the decision to over 1,000 analysts, shareholders, and industry experts the next day.
caveats: The Affymetrix case notes a two-quarter hit to market cap; the source frames the recall as a turning point in customer relationships, but that outcome followed transparent disclosure and staff alignment, not the recall alone.
Two arduous days of debate is a source-specific illustration, not a required duration.
cards.source_name: Multipliers_ How the Best Leaders Make Everyone Smarter.docx
